newsitem.title: INDIA: Acknowledge Kashmir dispute, Pakistan tells India.
newsitem.headline: Acknowledge Kashmir dispute, Pakistan tells India.

text.p: Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan has asked India to acknowledge the existence of a bilateral dispute over Kashmir, saying such a move was a key condition for improving relations.

Khan was quoted by the Times of India on Monday as dismissing suggestions in the Indian media that the Kashmir issue could be put on hold in order to allow the arch-foes to resolve less intractable disputes first.
Khan said he had raised the issue with Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral when the two met in New Delhi earlier this month. Gujral was India's foreign minister at that time.

"He told me that he had had a meeting with the U.N. secretary general (Kofi Annan) and had told him that even if you have to defrost a refrigerator, it takes time. There are no quick fixes," Khan told the newspaper in an interview.
"So I told Mr Gujral in this meeting, 'It's good that you recognise there is a refrigerator to defreeze.' And that refrigerator is Kashmir."
India and Pakistan have fought two of their three wars since independence from Britain in 1947 over Kashmir. India controls two thirds of the region. Pakistan has the rest.
Gujral was due to meet Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif in Male next month on the fringes of a regional summit.
India says the state of Jammu and Kashmir is an integral part of the union and cannot be negotiated.
Pakistan presses its case by citing a 1949 U.N. resolution calling for a plebisite by Kashmiris to determine if they wish to stay with India or go to Pakistan.

"From Pakistan's point of view the core issue is always Jammu and Kashmir. India keeps saying it is part of the Indian Union and so says its constitution," Khan said, adding that India could change its constitution as other countries do.

"So that's not really a solid argument. Kashmir is an internationally recognised dispute. We feel strongly that the two of us have got bogged down in a straitjacket, fought three wars -- to what end?"
Asked if Pakistan would reciprocate following India's recent move to ease bilateral travel restrictions, Khan said: "We will, slowly."

"There has to be de-freezing, as Mr Gujral said. We have to build confidence among ourselves, move to the recognition of the core issue on Kashmir, and you'll find Pakistanis landing up in large numbers in Delhi and your businessmen landing up in Pakistan."
